title: CRED Founder Kunal Shah Exits Board to Lead WhatsApp as Meta Invests $900 Million in His Fintech Startup
excerpt: Shah has stepped down as CRED promoter and board member after Meta named him WhatsApp's global CEO, capping an unusual deal that puts an Indian entrepreneur at the helm of the world's largest messaging platform.
body:
• Kunal Shah, 47, has stepped down as CRED's promoter and board member after Meta named him WhatsApp's new global CEO, replacing Will Cathcart
  • Meta invested approximately $900 million (₹8,550 crore) in CRED for a 20% stake, valuing the fintech startup at $4.5 billion
  • Shah retains about 20% ownership of CRED through personal and family holdings but will not hold an executive role at the company
  • The appointment puts an Indian founder at the helm of a platform with 3.3 billion monthly users, with India as its largest market at 500 million users

An Unusual Executive Crossover

Kunal Shah, the founder of Indian fintech unicorn CRED, has formally severed his management ties with the company after Meta Platforms named him WhatsApp's new global chief executive — a move that puts an Indian entrepreneur with no engineering degree or Silicon Valley pedigree in charge of the world's largest messaging app.

According to filings reviewed by Mint and lodged with India's Ministry of Corporate Affairs, Shah converted his 11.14% promoter shareholding into public shareholding on June 22 and resigned from the board of Dreamplug Technologies, CRED's holding company. He continues to own approximately 20% of the startup through his personal stake and his family investment vehicle, QED Innovation Labs LLP.

The governance transition coincided with Meta's $900 million investment in CRED, structured through a combination of primary and secondary share purchases. The deal values the Bengaluru-based credit card management company at $4.5 billion post-money — a recovery from an internal valuation that had dipped to $1.2 billion in December 2025.

"Cathcart will move to a new role at Meta focused on building products from scratch."

Why Meta Chose Shah

Meta's Chief Product Officer Chris Cox, who led the search, said the company was looking for a leader with "an intuitive grasp of the immense, global product potential for WhatsApp." In an internal memo reviewed by Reuters, Cox described Shah as having "immense entrepreneurial energy combined with a natural humanism."

"Kunal built CRED into one of India's most important technology companies, and he brings the kind of builder mentality and global perspective that will serve him well in running the world's biggest messaging app."

— Mark Zuckerberg, Meta CEO

Shah replaces Will Cathcart, who led WhatsApp since 2019 and oversaw its expansion to more than 100 million users in the United States. Cathcart will move to a new role at Meta focused on building products from scratch. Miten Sampat, who heads strategy and finance at CRED, has been appointed interim CEO while the board works on a longer-term leadership structure ahead of an eventual IPO.

India at the Centre of WhatsApp's Next Chapter

The appointment reflects Meta's strategic bet on India, WhatsApp's largest market with more than 500 million users — a significant share of the platform's 3.3 billion monthly active global user base. Industry executives say the move signals Meta's ambitions to deepen commerce and financial services offerings across emerging markets including India, Brazil, and Indonesia.

Shah has spent two decades building businesses around digital payments and consumer behaviour in India. Before CRED, he founded FreeCharge, a mobile payments platform he sold to Snapdeal. His track record in fintech is seen as central to WhatsApp's push to become a "superapp" that captures a bigger share of online payments — an area where WhatsApp Pay has gained traction in India but lagged behind local rivals PhonePe and Google Pay.

Meta said it would not receive a board seat at CRED or access to CRED's customer data under the terms of the investment. Shah, in his announcement, said the two companies would operate independently.

What It Means for CRED and Indian Tech

Shah's departure from CRED's board marks a clean break from the company he founded in 2018, though the scale of his continued ownership means his financial interests remain closely aligned with CRED's trajectory. The startup, backed by Peak XV Partners and Tiger Global, has been preparing for an eventual public listing.

For India's technology ecosystem, the appointment carries symbolic weight. Shah joins a small but growing roster of Indian-origin executives leading major global technology platforms, a trend that now extends from Google and Microsoft to the world's most widely used messaging service.

On social media platform X, Shah wrote: "While it's come very far, the delta between WhatsApp today and its full potential is massive." The statement signals an ambitious agenda at a time when the messaging platform is central to daily communication, business transactions, and increasingly, government services across much of the developing world.
